text: The first feathers were simple fuzz, like a chick's down. They probably kept small dinosaurs warm.
Later feathers grew branches and flat vanes. Dinosaurs likely used them for showing off, covering eggs and balancing as they ran.
Much later, some feathered dinosaurs began to glide and flap. Flying came second. Most feathered dinosaurs never left the ground, and some were far too big to fly, even with a full feathered coat.

keys.label: 1. Fuzz
keys.cap: Simple hollow threads, like a chick's down. Little Sinosauropteryx was covered in them. Probably for keeping warm.

keys.label: 2. Tufts
keys.cap: Bunches of threads growing from one spot. Fluffier and warmer.

keys.label: 3. Branches
keys.cap: A central shaft with branches. Good for colourful displays.

keys.label: 4. Vanes
keys.cap: Branches zip together into a flat vane. Caudipteryx had fans of these on its arms and tail, for showing off.

keys.label: 5. Flight feathers
keys.cap: Lopsided vanes that grip the air. Microraptor and early birds used them to glide and fly.

quiz.prompt: A tyrannosaur from China called Yutyrannus was about 9 m long. What did scientists find on its fossils?

Bony armour plates

quiz.reveal: Yutyrannus, described in 2012, was covered in long, simple filaments up to about 20 cm long. It lived in a cool climate, so the fluffy coat may have kept it warm. It showed that even big meat-eaters could be feathered.

sec.t:
Feathers are made of [[keratin|keratin]], the same stuff as your hair and nails. A flight feather has a central shaft with hundreds of branches that zip together with tiny hooks. The branches on the front edge are shorter than those at the back, so the vane is lopsided. That shape helps the feather slice through the air.

Simple feathers are different. They are just hollow threads, or tufts of threads, without hooks. Scientists think feathers [[evolve|evolved]] in steps, from threads to tufts to branched feathers to flat vanes. Living birds show the same order as they grow. A newly hatched chick is covered in fluffy down, and its stiff, flat feathers come in later. Feathers also wear out, so birds shed and regrow them, usually once or twice a year. Scientists are still searching [[fossil|fossils]] for clear signs that feathered dinosaurs moulted too.

Fine-grained volcanic ash in Liaoning, China, preserved dinosaurs with their feathers in extraordinary detail. Some even kept their [[@dino-colors|colour clues]]. The first feathered one, Sinosauropteryx, was found in 1996, covered in short fuzz along its back and tail.

Since then, dozens of feathered kinds have been found there. In 2012, scientists named Yutyrannus, a tyrannosaur about 9 m long, covered in long fluffy filaments. Its home had cool winters, so the coat may have kept it warm. A feathered tail tip has even turned up [[@amber-fossils|trapped in amber]] from Myanmar.

Microraptor, a crow-sized dinosaur from China, had long flight feathers on both its arms and its legs. It probably glided between trees. [[@velociraptor-real|Velociraptor]] had bumps on its arm bones where big feathers attached, even though it was too heavy to fly. Its ancestors may once have flown, or its feathers may have been for show.

Over time, some small feathered dinosaurs used their wings to flap and fly. Their [[descendant|descendants]] are today's birds.

That is still debated. A plant-eater from Siberia called Kulindadromeus, far from the bird branch, had fuzzy threads as well as scales. That suggests the ability to grow feather-like coverings might go back to the earliest dinosaurs. But skin prints from many big dinosaurs, including T. rex, show only scales. Perhaps some lost their fuzz as they grew large, the way elephants have very little hair.

Today, feathers keep birds warm and dry, help them fly, and help them show off. Owls even have soft-edged feathers that let them [[@owl-silent|fly in silence]].

text: Most big caves form in limestone, a rock made mostly of the remains of ancient sea creatures. When rain falls, it picks up a little [[@carbon-cycle|carbon dioxide]] from the air and soil, which turns it into a very weak [[acid|acid]], like a much gentler [[@soft-drinks|fizzy drink]].

That water seeps into cracks in the limestone and slowly [[dissolve|dissolves]] the rock. Over tens of thousands of years, tiny cracks widen into tunnels, and tunnels into caves. Some caves stretch for hundreds of kilometres underground.

d.try: Watch rock-like stuff dissolve. Put a clean piece of eggshell or a small seashell in a glass of kitchen vinegar, and another in plain water. Eggshells and seashells are made of calcite, the same mineral as limestone. Look closely. Tiny bubbles form on the one in vinegar as it slowly dissolves, a much faster version of what rainwater does underground.
myth: Caves are carved out quickly by fast underground rivers.

Most limestone caves begin very slowly, as slightly acidic water seeps through tiny cracks and dissolves the rock over tens of thousands of years or more. Streams may widen them later, but the first work is chemistry, not force.
facts: often a fraction of a millimetre a year

sec.t:
[[@rocks-types|Limestone]] is made of a [[@minerals-everyday|mineral called calcite]]. Pure water barely touches it. But slightly acidic water dissolves it, slowly, the way a sugar cube dissolves in tea, only millions of times slower.

Water follows the easiest path. It trickles down cracks and along the joins between rock layers, and dissolves the walls as it goes. Wider cracks carry more water, which dissolves more rock, so the biggest passages grow fastest. When the [[@groundwater|water table]], the level of water underground, drops, the passages drain and fill with air. Now there is a cave.

The same water that carves a cave also decorates it. When a drop of water carrying dissolved calcite seeps from a cave ceiling, it loses some of its [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] to the air. It can no longer hold all its calcite, so it leaves a tiny ring of it behind.

Drop by drop, the rings build down into a hanging stalactite. Where drops land on the floor, calcite builds up into a stalagmite. If the two meet, they form a column. One way to remember which is which: stalactites hold on *tight* to the ceiling, and stalagmites *might* reach it one day.

Most grow much more slowly than your fingernails, often by a fraction of a millimetre in a year. A metre-long stalactite may be thousands of years old.

{{story:bats-fly}}

India has many limestone caves. The Borra Caves, in the Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, are full of tall stalactites. The Belum Caves, also in Andhra Pradesh, wind for more than 3 km underground.

The longest caves in India lie in [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], in the rainy hills of [[@northeast-india|northeast India]]. Heavy rain and thick limestone have made hundreds of caves there. Krem Liat Prah, the longest, stretches for more than 30 km. Cavers from India and Britain have been mapping these caves together for decades.

[[mammoth|Mammoth]] Cave in Kentucky is the longest known cave system in the world, with more than 680 km of mapped passages. Layers of hard sandstone above the limestone acted like a roof, protecting the passages from collapse.

The biggest single cave passage known is Son Doong in [[@vietnam|Vietnam]]. Parts of it are big enough to fit a block of skyscrapers, and it has its own patch of jungle where the roof has fallen in. A local man, Ho Khanh, found its entrance in the early 1990s, and British cavers explored it in 2009.

Not every cave is dissolved limestone. [[lava|Lava]] tubes form when the outside of a lava flow cools and hardens while hot lava keeps flowing inside, leaving a hollow tube. [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]] has many. Sea caves are hollowed out by [[@cliffs-erosion|waves pounding cliffs]]. Ice caves form inside [[@glaciers|glaciers]], where meltwater carves tunnels.

When the roof of a limestone cave grows too thin, it can collapse and leave a hole called a [[@sinkholes|sinkhole]]. People have also made their own caves. The temples of [[@rashtrakutas|Ellora]] in Maharashtra were cut by hand into solid rock, including the [[@ellora-kailasa|Kailasa temple]], carved from the top down out of a single cliff.

text: From space, Earth looks like a brilliant blue ball swirled with white clouds, brown and green land and bright white ice at the poles. Oceans cover about 71% of the surface, so blue is the colour you notice first. A thin, glowing layer of air hugs the edge of the planet like a halo.

At night, the view changes completely. Cities glow orange and gold, linked by strings of light along highways and rivers. Lightning flickers inside storms, and green auroras ripple near the poles. Astronauts often say the view is the best part of their job, and many describe feeling protective of the planet after seeing it.

st.reveal: The Great Wall is very long but only a few metres wide, and built from local stone and earth, so it blends in. Astronauts say cities, airports, big roads and dams are far easier to spot. Chinese astronaut Yang Liwei said he couldn't see the wall at all.

myth: The Great Wall of China is the only human-made thing you can see from space.

From the space station, astronauts can see many human-made things, like cities, airports, dams and big farms, especially at night when city lights shine. The Great Wall is actually one of the hardest to spot, because it is so narrow.

sec.t:
The International [[@space-station|Space Station]] [[orbit|orbits]] about 400 kilometres above the ground, roughly the straight-line distance from Delhi to Lucknow, but straight up. It zooms around Earth in about 90 minutes. So astronauts see a sunrise or sunset roughly every 45 minutes, about 16 of each a day.

From that height, they can make out rivers, mountain ranges, deserts and big cities. The Himalaya look like a crumpled white sheet. The Thar Desert shows as a sandy patch next to the green fields of Punjab. Big dams, airports and even large ships' trails in the water are visible. [[hurricane|Hurricanes]] and [[@cyclones-india|cyclones]] look like giant spinning pinwheels.

In 1990, the [[@voyager|Voyager 1]] spacecraft was about 6 billion kilometres away, beyond Neptune's orbit. At the suggestion of [[astronomer|astronomer]] Carl Sagan, NASA turned its camera back towards home. In the photo, Earth is a tiny speck, less than a single [[pixel|pixel]], caught in a beam of scattered sunlight.

Sagan called it the Pale Blue Dot. He pointed out that every person who has ever lived spent their life on that speck. The photo is still shown in classrooms to give a sense of how small and precious our world is.

In 1984, Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian in space, flying on a Soviet mission. Prime Minister Indira Gandhi spoke to him by video link and asked how India looked from space. He replied with a line from a famous song: "Saare Jahan Se Achha", better than all the world.

Kalpana Chawla, born in Karnal, flew on two NASA space shuttle missions. In 2025, Shubhanshu Shukla became the first Indian astronaut to visit the space station. Their photos and stories have brought the view home to millions of Indian children. Sunita Williams, an American astronaut whose father came from Gujarat, has spent hundreds of days on the space station too.

One thing astronauts notice is what they can't see: borders between countries. Rivers, coastlines and mountains are clear, but the lines on a map are invisible. The writer Frank White called the feeling of seeing Earth this way the overview effect.

Satellites now photograph every part of Earth every few days. Indian [[@satellites-india|satellites]] track crops, forests, floods and fishing zones. The view from space isn't only beautiful. It helps farmers, scientists and rescue teams on the ground.

text: AstroSat is India's first space [[observatory|observatory]] built for astronomy, a satellite carrying several telescopes that study the universe. ISRO launched it on 28 September 2015, on a PSLV rocket from [[@launch-sites|Sriharikota]]. It circles Earth about 650 km up.

Its special skill is seeing many kinds of light at once. Stars, [[galaxy|galaxies]] and black holes give off visible light, but also [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light and X-rays, which our eyes can't see and which Earth's air blocks. AstroSat carries five instruments, so it can watch the same object in ultraviolet, visible light and X-rays at the same time.
That is useful because many things in space change quickly. Watching them across several kinds of light at once shows what is really happening.

st.prompt: Why does AstroSat have to be in space to see X-rays and most ultraviolet light from stars?

options.t: Earth's atmosphere blocks them before they reach the ground
They only exist far away from Earth
Telescopes on the ground are too small

st.reveal: Our atmosphere soaks up X-rays and most ultraviolet light, which is lucky for us, because both can harm living things. But it means astronomers must send telescopes above the air to see the universe in these kinds of light.

d.try: Shine a TV remote at a phone camera and press a button. Many phone cameras can see the remote's flashing infrared light, which your eyes can't. Telescopes like AstroSat work the same way, using special detectors to see light that is invisible to us.
myth: Space telescopes are useful because they are closer to the stars.
A few hundred kilometres makes no real difference to distances of light-years. Telescopes go to space to get above the air, which blurs visible light and blocks X-rays and much ultraviolet light.

sec.t:
Light from space comes in many forms, from radio waves to visible light to X-rays. They are all the same kind of energy with different [[wavelength|wavelengths]], like notes on a very long piano. Our eyes only see a narrow middle part, the [[@colour-mix|colours]] of the rainbow.

Earth's [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] protects us by soaking up [[@x-rays|X-rays]] and most ultraviolet light. That is good for our skin and eyes, but bad for [[astronomer|astronomers]] who want to see those kinds of light. So, like NASA's [[@hubble|Hubble]], AstroSat works from above the air.

AstroSat's ultraviolet telescope, called UVIT, takes sharp pictures of hot young stars and distant galaxies. Its detectors were made with help from the Canadian Space Agency.

Three X-ray instruments measure X-rays of different energies. One of them, LAXPC, is especially good at catching rapid flickers from matter swirling around [[@black-holes|black holes]] and dense, dead stars called neutron stars. A fifth instrument scans the sky for sudden X-ray outbursts so the others can turn and look.

The instruments were built by ISRO with research institutes across India, including TIFR in Mumbai, the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru, IUCAA in Pune and the Raman Research Institute. The University of Leicester in the UK helped with one of the X-ray cameras.

{{story:x-rays}}

In 2020, a team led by astronomers at IUCAA reported that UVIT had detected extreme ultraviolet light from a galaxy called AUDFs01. The galaxy is about 9.3 billion [[@light-years|light-years]] away, so that light left it long before the Sun and Earth formed.

Light like this is easily absorbed on its long journey. Catching it helps scientists understand how early galaxies lit up the gas around them, a big question about how the universe changed after the [[@big-bang|Big Bang]].

AstroSat has also studied star clusters, the leftovers of exploded stars and the flashes from black holes eating gas from neighbouring stars.

AstroSat was designed to last about five years, but it kept working long after that. Scientists from India and around the world can send in proposals to use it, and a committee decides who gets observing time. Students at Indian universities have written their research on its data.

Since then, India has launched two more space observatories. Aditya-L1, launched in 2023, studies the Sun. XPoSat, launched on 1 January 2024, measures the direction in which X-rays from bright cosmic sources vibrate, which tells scientists about the magnetic fields around black holes and neutron stars. Each one was carried into [[orbit|orbit]] from Sriharikota by an [[@isro-launch|ISRO rocket]].

text: Maybe, but nobody has proved it. In 2012, a team led by Nikku Madhusudhan, an Indian-born [[astronomer|astronomer]] then at Yale University, studied a planet called 55 Cancri e. Its star seemed rich in carbon, and the planet's size and weight fitted a world made largely of carbon. Under deep pressure, they suggested, as much as a third of it might be diamond.

Headlines called it the "diamond planet". But later studies found the star may not be as carbon-rich as thought, and in 2024 the James Webb Space Telescope detected hints of an [[atmosphere|atmosphere]] on the planet. Today, many astronomers think its interior is more like Earth's rock than a diamond. That's how science often works: a bold idea gets tested, and the evidence decides.

st.prompt: What does a planet need to have a lot of diamond inside it?

options.t: Lots of carbon and enormous pressure
Lots of water and cold temperatures
A very bright star

st.reveal: Diamond is just carbon squeezed so hard that its atoms lock into a strong crystal. On Earth, this happens about 150 km underground. A carbon-rich planet with deep, crushing pressure could, in theory, hold huge amounts of it.

sec.t:
55 Cancri e circles its star so closely that a full year there lasts about 18 hours. You'd have a birthday every day, with time left over. It's about twice as wide as Earth and about eight times heavier, so it's called a super-Earth.

It's also blisteringly hot. Its dayside reaches over 2,000 °C, hot enough to melt many rocks, so its surface may be partly covered in a [[lava|lava]] ocean. The planet is probably tidally locked, with one side always facing its star, just as the Moon always shows the same face to Earth.

Its star, 55 Cancri, is about 41 [[@light-years|light-years]] away, in the [[constellation|constellation]] Cancer. On a very dark night far from city lights, it's just barely visible without a telescope.

sec.h: A star like a giant gem
sec.t:
Astronomers have found a dead star that might be even more sparkly. When stars like the Sun die, they shrink into white dwarfs, about the size of Earth. As they cool over billions of years, the carbon and oxygen inside can freeze into crystals.

One white dwarf, BPM 37093, nicknamed "Lucy", has a core thought to be largely crystallised. It's sometimes compared to a diamond as wide as a planet, though its crystals are packed differently from diamonds on Earth. Our own Sun may end this way in about 5 billion years, part of the [[@star-life-cycle|life cycle of stars]].

On Earth, natural diamonds form about 150 km underground and are carried up by volcanic eruptions. India was the world's only known source of diamonds for many centuries, from the Golconda mines that produced the famous [[@kohinoor|Kohinoor]].

In space, carbon is the fourth most common [[element|element]]. Tiny nanodiamonds have been found inside [[meteorite|meteorites]], older than the Sun itself. So diamond worlds aren't impossible, just unproven. With better [[@exoplanets|exoplanet]] studies, astronomers may yet find one that really sparkles.

text: A rogue planet is a planet that doesn't [[orbit|orbit]] a star. It drifts alone through the [[galaxy|galaxy]], in darkness and bitter cold. Most were probably born around a star like any other planet, then flung out into space by the gravity of bigger neighbours. Some may have formed on their own from a collapsing cloud of gas.

They are very hard to see, because they give off almost no light. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] find them by watching for a rare trick of [[gravity|gravity]], when a rogue planet passes in front of a far-off star and makes it briefly brighter. From the few they've found, scientists guess there could be billions or even trillions in the Milky Way.

st.prompt: A rogue planet gives off almost no light. How do astronomers spot one?

options.t: Its gravity briefly bends and brightens the light of a star behind it
It blocks out stars like a black dot
It reflects sunlight from a nearby star

st.reveal: When a rogue planet drifts in front of a distant star, its gravity acts like a lens and makes the star look brighter for a few hours or days. This is called microlensing.

src: Sumi T. et al. (2023) Free-floating planet mass function from MOA-II 9-year survey towards the Galactic bulge, The Astronomical Journal.

n.certNote: Rogue planets have definitely been found, mostly by a method called microlensing. But how many exist is uncertain. Estimates range from billions to trillions in the Milky Way, and some objects are hard to tell apart from failed stars.

myth: A rogue planet is on its way to crash into Earth.

Stories about a hidden planet called Nibiru are not true. Astronomers would easily see any planet close enough to threaten us. Space is so empty that a rogue planet passing near the Sun is extremely unlikely.

sec.t:
Young [[solar-system|solar systems]] are messy. Planets form in a spinning disc of gas and dust. Some grow big, like Jupiter, and their gravity tugs hard on the smaller ones. A small planet that wanders too close to a giant can be slingshot right out of the system, like a ball whacked out of a cricket ground.

Computer models suggest our own solar system may have lost a planet or two this way, billions of years ago. If so, it is still out there somewhere, frozen and drifting. Flung planets don't slow down much, because space has almost nothing to rub against. A planet thrown out at a few kilometres per second would keep that speed for billions of years, crossing the gaps between stars one slow step at a time.

sec.h: Finding a planet you can't see

sec.t:
On 30 August 2026, NASA launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope on a Falcon Heavy rocket from Florida. Roman can see an area of sky about 100 times bigger than Hubble can in one shot. Astronomers expect it to find hundreds of rogue planets, some as small as Mars.

That will give the first proper count. It will help answer a big question: are lonely planets rare oddballs, or are they the most common kind of planet in the galaxy?

In 2023, astronomers using the [[@webb-telescope|Webb telescope]] spotted dozens of objects about the mass of Jupiter floating free in the Orion Nebula. Some seemed to come in pairs, orbiting each other with no star. They were nicknamed JuMBOs, for Jupiter-mass [[binary|binary]] objects.

Not everyone is convinced. Some astronomers think many could be faint background stars or galaxies. Further study is under way, and it shows how tricky it is to spot dark objects in space.

A rogue planet's surface would be colder than −200°C, with no sunrise, ever. But a planet keeps some heat inside from when it formed, and [[radioactive|radioactive]] rocks keep warming it. Under a thick layer of ice or a heavy atmosphere, that heat might keep an ocean liquid for billions of years.

It's only an idea for now. But Jupiter's moon Europa already has an ocean under its ice, warmed from within, far from the Sun's heat. Scientists wonder whether life needs a sun at all. And if our own Sun [[@what-if-sun-vanished|vanished tomorrow]], Earth would sail off in a straight line and become a rogue planet too.

text: Birds [[migration|migrate]] to follow food and good weather. In winter, insects become hard to find in northern Asia, but in southern Africa it is summer and insects are everywhere. So the Amur falcon, a bird weighing about 150 g, flies from China, Mongolia and Russia to southern Africa every autumn and back again in spring.

On the way, lakhs of them stop in Nagaland in [[@northeast-india|Northeast India]] to rest and feast on insects. Then they cross India and fly out over the Arabian Sea, non-stop for days, without landing. Scientists learned their route by fixing tiny satellite tags on a few birds.

sec.h: A village that changed its mind
sec.t:
Around 2012, conservationists reported that huge numbers of Amur falcons were being trapped for food near Doyang lake in Nagaland's Wokha district. The news spread around the world. Local villages, especially Pangti, decided to protect the birds instead. Village councils banned hunting, children joined eco-clubs, and the state government and conservation groups helped.

Now the falcons roost safely, and visitors come each October to watch clouds of birds settle into the trees at dusk. Some people call the area the falcon capital of the world.

India is a winter home for millions of migrating birds. From October, ducks, cranes, storks and waders arrive from Central Asia, Siberia and Europe. In the village of Khichan in Rajasthan, thousands of demoiselle cranes land each winter, and villagers have fed them grain for decades. Siberian cranes once wintered at Keoladeo National Park in Bharatpur, but the last ones were seen there in 2002.

Before setting off, many birds eat huge amounts and store the energy as fat. Some small songbirds nearly double their weight. During the flight their bodies burn this fat like fuel, and some even shrink parts of their gut to save weight. When they arrive, they are thin and very hungry.

Amur falcons are not the only great travellers. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas, as you can read in [[@bar-headed-goose|how geese cross the mountains]]. [[@sky-arctic-tern|Arctic terns]] fly from [[@arctic|the Arctic]] to the Antarctic and back each year, covering about 70,000 km and chasing a second summer. In 2022, a young bar-tailed godwit tracked by scientists flew about 13,500 km non-stop from [[@alaska|Alaska]] to Tasmania, without eating or resting.

Insects migrate too. Some scientists think Amur falcons may feed on swarms of migrating dragonflies over the Arabian Sea, which you can read about in [[@insect-flight|insect flight]]. Nobody has proved it yet, but it would explain how such small birds keep going so far from land.

text: Country music is a style of American popular music that grew out of the folk songs of the rural South, especially the [[@appalachians|Appalachian]] mountains. It is known for story-telling lyrics about everyday life, love, family, hard work, faith and small towns. Its sound comes from the fiddle, banjo, acoustic [[@guitar|guitar]] and the sliding, crying steel guitar.

Its roots lie in the ballads brought by settlers from [[@scotland|Scotland]], Ireland and England, mixed with the banjo and musical styles of African Americans. In the 1920s, radio and records turned these local sounds into a national music. Today country is one of the best-selling kinds of music in the United States, centred on Nashville, Tennessee.

st.prompt: The Grand Ole Opry radio show began in Nashville in 1925. Is it still on air?

options.t: Yes, it has been broadcast every week for over a century
No, it ended when television arrived
It stopped in the 1950s and restarted online

st.reveal: The Opry has gone out on the radio every week since 1925, making it one of the longest-running radio shows in the world. Being invited to join its cast is still one of the highest honours in country music.

Black musicians helped shape country music from the start. The banjo has African roots, the harmonica player DeFord Bailey was one of the first stars of the Grand Ole Opry, and singers such as Charley Pride and, more recently, Beyoncé have topped the country charts.

sec.t:
In the 1700s and 1800s, many settlers from Scotland, Ireland and England made homes in the Appalachian mountains. They brought old ballads, long songs that told stories of love, murder and adventure, and dance tunes played on the fiddle.

In the American South, they met the music of enslaved Africans and their [[descendant|descendants]]. The banjo came from African instruments made of a gourd and a skin, with a long neck. Black musicians also brought [[rhythm|rhythms]], the bluesy sliding notes and new ways of singing. Mixed together over generations, these sounds became "old-time" or "hillbilly" music, played at dances, churches and on porches.

In 1925, a radio station in Nashville started a Saturday night show of fiddle and string-band music. It became the Grand Ole Opry. Families across the South gathered around their radios to listen, and singers who appeared on it became famous.

The Opry is still broadcast every week, making it one of the longest-running [[@radio-shows|radio shows]] in the world. Nashville grew into the home of country music recording, and is now nicknamed Music City.

Country music has many branches. Bluegrass, created by Bill Monroe in the 1940s, is fast and acoustic, with brilliant banjo and fiddle playing. Honky-tonk, made famous by Hank Williams, is the sound of bars and broken hearts. Johnny Cash sang about prisoners and the poor, and Dolly Parton wrote hits including "Jolene" and "9 to 5".

Modern country often blends with pop and rock. [[@taylor-swift|Taylor Swift]] began as a teenage country singer before moving to pop. In 2019, Lil Nas X's country-rap song "Old Town Road" spent 19 weeks at number one in the US. In 2025, Beyoncé's country album *Cowboy Carter* won the Grammy for Album of the Year.

Country music has a loyal following in parts of north-east India, especially in Meghalaya and Nagaland, where Western music has been loved for generations. In [[@shillong|Shillong]], local bands play country and rock songs at cafés and festivals. Its songs about land, family and home have a lot in common with India's own [[@folk-music-india|folk songs]].

text: Most people today would say yes, photography can be art. Major museums collect photographs, art schools teach photography, and some photos sell for huge sums.

But it wasn't always so obvious. A camera records what is in front of it, so early critics argued it was a machine doing the work, not an artist. Photographers replied that the art lies in choosing: what to point at, how to frame it, when to press the button and how to print it. That argument has been going on since photography began, and in a way it still is. Not every photo is art, just as not every drawing is.

st.prompt: Two people photograph the same tree on the same day. Why might one picture be called art and the other not?

options.t: Because of the choices made, such as framing, light, timing and what the picture makes you feel
Because one used a more expensive camera
Because one was printed bigger

st.reveal: Photographers choose where to stand, what to leave out, when to press the shutter and how to edit. Those decisions shape what you notice and feel, which is why the same subject can look ordinary or unforgettable.

sec.h: A machine that draws with light
sec.t:
The oldest surviving photograph taken with a camera was made in France around 1826 by Nicéphore Niépce. It shows rooftops seen from his window, and needed hours of exposure. In 1839 Louis Daguerre announced a faster process in [[@paris|Paris]], and photography spread around the world within months. You can read more in [[@photography-history|How did the first photographs change the world?]].

For portraits, a photograph was faster and cheaper than a painting. Many portrait painters lost work. Some critics worried that painting itself would no longer be needed.

In New York in the early 1900s, the photographer Alfred Stieglitz ran galleries that showed photographs alongside modern paintings. He argued hard that they belonged together. In 1940 the Museum of Modern Art opened a department of photography, one of the first in a major art museum.

In the United States, Ansel Adams became famous for black-and-white photographs of [[@national-parks|national parks]] like [[@yosemite|Yosemite]], with huge mountains and glowing skies. He planned each picture carefully, from where to stand to how long to develop the print, so the final image matched what he had in mind.

Photography reached India in the 1840s. In the late 1800s Lala Deen Dayal photographed palaces, monuments and royal courts, and became court photographer to the Nizam of [[@hyderabad|Hyderabad]].

In the 1940s, Homai Vyarawalla became India's first woman photojournalist. She photographed the last days of British rule and the early years of independence, including the leaders who shaped the new country. Today many Indian photographers' work hangs in galleries across the world. Satyajit Ray, before becoming a [[@satyajit-ray|great film-maker]], also worked in design and illustration, and his films show a photographer's eye for framing.

With [[@smartphones|smartphones]], billions of people carry a camera all the time. Estimates suggest well over a trillion photos are taken every year. Most are quick snaps of friends, food and holidays, not art.

That flood of pictures has made the old question interesting again. If anyone can take a sharp, colourful photo, what makes one special? Most photographers would give the same answer as in the 1800s: the seeing, not the machine.

text: The Taj Mahal in Agra was built by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife, Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. Work began around 1632 and took about 20 years, with around 20,000 workers: stone-carvers, masons, inlay artists and calligraphers.

Its white marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan, more than 300 km away. Elephants, bullocks and long earth ramps helped move the stone. The result looks almost weightless, a white dome floating above the Yamuna river.

st.prompt: Why are the Taj Mahal's four minarets tilted slightly outward?

options.t: The builders made a mistake
So that in an earthquake they'd fall away from the tomb
The ground is sinking

st.reveal: The commonly given reason is that the slight outward tilt means a falling minaret would topple away from the main tomb. It also makes them look straighter from the ground.

d.try: Fold a sheet of paper in half and open it again. Drop a few blobs of paint on one side of the fold, close the paper and press it flat with your hand. Open it to find a perfectly balanced design. Now try painting half a building with a dome and towers, then fold and press to complete the other half.
myth: Shah Jahan had the workers' hands cut off so they could never build anything as beautiful again.
This is a popular legend, and historians have found no evidence for it. Ustad Ahmad Lahauri, the architect usually credited with the Taj, is also credited with Shah Jahan's later Red Fort in Delhi.

sec.t:
The Taj is almost perfectly symmetrical. Its left side mirrors its right, the four [[minaret|minarets]] stand at equal distances, and a long pool in the garden reflects the whole building. The garden itself is a *charbagh*, a Persian-style garden split into four parts by water channels.

There is one famous break in the pattern. Mumtaz Mahal's tomb lies exactly at the centre. When Shah Jahan died in 1666, he was buried beside her, slightly off to one side. It is the only thing in the whole design that isn't balanced. Even the red sandstone buildings on either side match. A mosque stands on the west, and an almost identical building on the east, called the *jawab* or "answer", is there mainly to balance it. The same love of [[@symmetry|symmetry]] appears in a [[@rangoli-symmetry|kolam]] drawn at a South Indian doorstep.

The flowers on the walls aren't painted. They are thin slices of coloured stone, such as carnelian, jasper and lapis lazuli, cut to shape and fitted into hollows carved in the marble. This art is called *pietra dura* in Italian and *parchin kari* in Persian and Hindi.

Some single flowers contain dozens of pieces, fitted so tightly that the joins are hard to see. Some stones came from far away, such as lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, the same blue stone that the painters of [[@ajanta-colours|Ajanta]] used centuries earlier. Families of craftspeople in Agra still practise the art, making tabletops and boxes for visitors. Their skills link them to the [[@mughals|Mughal]] workshops of nearly 400 years ago.

Marble is a soft stone that reacts with [[acid|acids]]. Dust, soot and polluted air slowly stain it yellow and brown. In the 1990s, India's Supreme Court ordered many industries around Agra to switch to cleaner fuels or move away, and polluting vehicles are kept away from the monument.

To clean the walls, restorers spread a paste of *multani mitti*, a fine clay also used in face packs, and leave it to dry. When it is washed off, it pulls dirt out of the marble's tiny pores. The Taj became a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1983, and millions of people visit every year. Keeping it white is a job that never quite ends.

text: India gets most of its oil from other countries. It buys a thick, dark liquid called crude oil from places like Russia, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and the USA, brings it home on huge ships, and turns it into petrol, diesel and cooking gas in its own refineries.

India is the world's third-biggest user of oil, after the USA and China. But it pumps only a small part of what it needs from its own wells. So where it buys oil, and how much it pays, affects prices for almost everyone.

quiz.prompt: If the price of crude oil jumps around the world, what usually happens in India a few weeks later?

options.t: Petrol, diesel and bus fares tend to cost more, and so do many goods that travel by truck
Nothing changes, because India makes all its own oil
Only aeroplane tickets change, because cars do not use crude oil

quiz.reveal: India buys most of its oil from abroad and pays in dollars. When crude gets dearer, refineries pay more, fuel prices tend to rise, and trucks charge more to carry vegetables, milk and parcels. That is why one faraway oil price can show up in a family's monthly budget.

news.h: US pauses its tariff threat over India's Russian oil and links it to a trade deal
news.t: On 16 October 2026, US President Donald Trump paused parts of a new US law that allowed tariffs of up to 100% on goods from big buyers of Russian oil, including India and China. India is the second-biggest buyer of Russian oil, after China. Speaking in Uzbekistan on 19 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the nearly finished India-US trade deal was one of the things the US weighed. He had also said India could not switch away from Russian oil overnight. Rubio arrived in Mumbai on 20 October. India buys more than 85% of the crude oil it uses from abroad, so who sells it that oil, and at what price, matters to every family. This entry explains where India's oil comes from and why it is such a big question.

sec.t:
Oil is bought and sold all over the world, a bit like vegetables in one giant market. Prices are set in US dollars, and they go up and down every day.

Here is the journey of the oil in a scooter's tank:

1. An oil company in another country pumps crude oil out of the ground.
2. An Indian refinery buys it, often months in advance, and pays in dollars, a foreign [[currency|currency]].
3. A giant ship called a tanker carries it across the sea to a port like Jamnagar, Paradip or Kochi.
4. A [[@oil-refinery|refinery]] heats the crude and splits it into petrol, diesel, jet fuel, cooking gas and more.
5. Pipelines, trains and trucks take the fuel to petrol pumps and gas agencies.

Think of a family that grows no wheat but eats rotis every day. It must keep buying wheat from the market, and if the price goes up, the family has to pay. India is in the same spot with oil.

Many ships pass through narrow sea lanes on the way. The most famous is the Strait of Hormuz, near Iran, where a large share of the world's oil sails out of the Gulf. When there is trouble there, oil prices can jump overnight.

Oil formed over millions of years from tiny sea creatures buried under mud and rock, as the story of [[@oil-coal|how coal and oil were made]] explains.

India's own oil story began in 1889, when a well was drilled at Digboi in Assam. A refinery opened there in 1901, and it still works today. In 1974, scientists found a big oil field under the sea off Mumbai, called Mumbai High. In 2004, a large field was found in the desert of Barmer in Rajasthan.

But India's need for fuel grew far faster than its wells. More cars, buses, tractors, planes and factories meant more and more oil had to be bought from abroad. Goods bought from other countries like this are called [[import|imports]].

{{story:oil-coal}}

For many years, India bought most of its oil from countries around the Gulf, such as Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the UAE. They were close, and their oil suited Indian refineries.

That changed after 2022, when Russia went to war with Ukraine. Western countries stopped buying much Russian oil, so Russia sold it cheaper to others. India bought a lot more, and Russia became one of its biggest suppliers.

This upset the USA. In August 2025, it put an extra 25% [[tariff|tariff]] on many Indian goods because of the Russian oil. That extra tariff was removed in February 2026, as the two countries worked on a trade deal. Later in 2026, a new US law allowed tariffs of up to 100% on the biggest buyers of Russian oil. In October 2026, the US paused that threat while it worked on a trade deal with India.

India's leaders say they buy oil where it is cheapest and most reliable for 140 crore people. They have also started buying more from the USA and from Venezuela, to spread the risk. Spreading purchases across many sellers is like a shop that keeps several suppliers, so one problem does not empty its shelves.

India also keeps emergency oil in huge underground rock caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur. These stores can keep the country going for some days if supplies are cut.

- **More than 85%**: the share of its crude oil that India buys from abroad. Fewer than 15 litres in every 100 come from Indian wells.
- **159 litres**: the size of one barrel, the unit oil is sold in. India uses millions of barrels every single day.
- **Third**: India's place among the world's oil users, after the USA and China.
- **About 157 dollars**: the record price of a barrel of the crude India buys, reached in March 2026 during a war in West Asia that shut the Strait of Hormuz. In calmer years the price has often been well under 100 dollars.

One debate is about who to buy from. Some say India should always buy the cheapest oil, wherever it comes from, because that keeps prices low for families. Others say India must also think about its friendships with big trading partners like the USA, who may punish countries that buy from Russia.

Another debate is about the future. Some want India to cut its oil needs fast, with [[@electric-cars|electric cars]], solar power and [[@ethanol-fuel|fuel made from sugarcane]]. Others point out that buses, trucks and planes will need oil for many years, so India should also look for more oil at home.

**"Crude oil and petrol are the same thing."** Crude oil is a thick mix straight from the ground. It must be cleaned and split in a refinery before it becomes petrol.

**"Oil prices only matter to people who drive."** Trucks carry food, medicine and parcels. When fuel costs more, so do many things in the shops.

**"India could just stop importing oil tomorrow."** Switching would take many years and huge amounts of money. That is why governments plan these changes slowly.

Every time you ride a bus, eat vegetables that came by truck, or see the blue flame of a gas stove, oil from far away is part of the story.

When world oil prices rise, the government and oil companies must decide how much of the extra cost to pass on. Higher fuel prices can push up [[@inflation|prices in general]], which is why the news watches oil so closely. India pays for oil in dollars, so a weak rupee makes it dearer too. Learning [[@trade-world|why countries trade]] helps explain why one war or one deal far away can change what your family pays at the petrol pump.

text: A vet, short for veterinarian, is a doctor for animals. Vets check animals for illness, give [[vaccine|vaccines]], set broken bones, do operations and advise owners on food and care. Some look after pets like dogs, cats and rabbits. Others care for cows, goats, horses and chickens on farms, or for wild animals in zoos and forests.
Vets also protect people. Many diseases, such as rabies and bird flu, can pass from animals to humans, so vets help stop outbreaks before they spread.

st.prompt: A vet needs to examine a wild tiger. What usually happens first?

options.t: The tiger is put to sleep with a dart
Keepers hold the tiger still by its paws
The vet waits until the tiger is very old

st.reveal: Wildlife vets use a dart gun to give a careful dose of sedative. Once the tiger is asleep, they check it quickly while a team watches its breathing, then let it wake up safely.

d.try: Watch a pet or a street animal you know, from a safe distance, for ten minutes. Note how it breathes, walks, eats and rests. Vets learn to spot illness by knowing what normal looks like, so write down three things that seem normal for that animal.
myth: A dog with a warm, dry nose must be ill.
A dog's nose can be warm or dry for many harmless reasons, such as sleeping or sitting in the sun. Vets look at other signs, like eating, energy and behaviour, to tell if a dog is unwell.

sec.t:
A human doctor can ask, "Where does it hurt?" A vet can't. Instead, vets watch how an animal stands, breathes, eats and moves. They feel its belly, listen to its heart with a stethoscope and check its eyes, ears and teeth.

They also listen carefully to owners, who know what is normal for their animal. When they need more clues, vets take blood tests or X-rays, just as hospitals do for people. A limping dog might have a thorn in its paw, a sprain or a broken bone, and only careful checks will tell. Size adds to the puzzle. A dose of medicine that helps a horse could harm a kitten, so vets work out doses carefully for each animal's weight and [[species|species]].

A pet clinic day often starts with check-ups and [[@vaccines|vaccines]]. Puppies and kittens need several jabs in their first months to protect them from diseases like rabies. Then come appointments: a cat that has stopped eating, a parrot plucking its feathers, a rabbit with overgrown teeth.

In the afternoon there may be operations, often neutering, which stops animals having unplanned babies. Emergencies can come at any time. A dog hit by a car or a cow struggling to give birth won't wait for office hours.

The world's first veterinary school opened in Lyon, France, in 1761, partly to fight cattle diseases. Today, in India, students usually study for about five and a half years, including an internship, for a degree called BVSc and AH. They must register with the Veterinary Council of India or a state council to practise.

In the United States, students first go to college and then spend four more years at vet school to earn a DVM degree, followed by a licensing exam. Getting in is competitive. Students study [[anatomy|anatomy]], medicine and surgery for many species, much as [[@jobs-doctor|doctors]] do for one.

Being a vet isn't only cuddling puppies. Vets see animals in pain, deal with worried or upset owners and sometimes have to put a very sick animal to sleep. They also risk bites, scratches and kicks.

Many vets say the best part is seeing an animal recover and go home. If you want to try it, helping at an animal shelter with an adult, or learning about [[@pets-care|pet care]], is a good start. In villages across India, a vet's visit to a sick [[@cows-india|cow]] can mean a family's milk and money for the year are safe.

text: People do sums in their heads by turning hard problems into easier ones. Instead of lining numbers up in columns the way you might on paper, they round them, split them into pieces, or use number facts they already know by heart.

For example, 49 + 37 is awkward. But 50 + 37 is easy: 87. Then you take away the extra 1 to get 86. Your brain can only juggle a few things at once, so good mental maths keeps each step small. Shopkeepers, cricket scorers, cooks and carpenters do this kind of thing every day, often without thinking of it as maths at all.

st.prompt: What is the quickest way to work out 25 × 16 in your head?

options.t: Halve 16 and double 25 until it's easy, 50 × 8, then 100 × 4 = 400
Write it out as long multiplication in your mind
Add 25 sixteen times

st.reveal: Doubling one number and halving the other keeps the answer the same. 25 × 16 becomes 50 × 8, then 100 × 4, which is easy. Mental maths is mostly about turning hard sums into friendly ones.

d.try: Play "shopkeeper" with a family member. Pick three items with prices, like ₹48, ₹27 and ₹19, and add them in your head using rounding (50 + 30 + 20, then take away the extra). Then work out the change from ₹100 by counting up. Swap roles and see who can explain their method best.
myth: People who are fast at mental maths have special brains and can't explain how they do it.
Most fast calculators use methods that can be learned, such as rounding, splitting numbers and remembering lots of number facts. Practice makes these steps quick, but they can describe them.

sec.t:
Rounding is the most useful trick. To add ₹198 and ₹56, think ₹200 + ₹56 = ₹256, then take away 2 to get ₹254. To subtract 97 from 340, take away 100 to get 240, then add back 3 to get 243.

This works because round numbers, like 10, 50, 100 and 1,000, are easy to add and subtract. You change the problem into a friendly one, then fix the small difference. It is also a quick way to check whether an answer on a calculator or a bill looks about right, which is called [[@estimation|estimation]].

Another trick is to break a number into pieces. To work out 7 × 46, split 46 into 40 and 6. Then 7 × 40 is 280 and 7 × 6 is 42. Add them: 322.

Mental [[@calculators|calculators]] often work from left to right, the opposite of school column methods. Starting with the biggest part gives you a good idea of the answer early on, and the small parts just tweak it. Knowing your [[@times-tables-tricks|times tables]] well makes every one of these steps faster.

Shakuntala Devi, born in Bengaluru in 1929, learned card tricks with her father as a small child and soon showed an astonishing gift for numbers. She toured the world doing calculations on stage.

On 18 June 1980, at Imperial College London, she was given two 13-digit numbers chosen by a computer. She multiplied them in her head and gave the 26-digit answer in 28 seconds. The feat entered the Guinness Book of Records. She also wrote books to help children enjoy maths, and always said her methods could be learned.

In Japan, China, India and elsewhere, many children learn to calculate on an [[@abacus|abacus]], sliding beads on rods. After years of practice, some stop using the real one. They picture it in their minds and move the imaginary beads, often twitching their fingers in the air. In Japan, this is called anzan.

Expert users can add long lists of numbers flashed on a screen faster than most people can read them. Researchers think it works because the mind turns numbers into pictures, and pictures are easier to hold in memory than strings of digits.

Phones can do any sum in a flash, so why train your brain? One reason is speed in everyday life: working out a bill, the time left before a train, or runs needed per over in a cricket chase. Another is catching mistakes. If you know roughly what an answer should be, you'll notice when a machine or a person gets it wrong.

Mental maths also builds number sense, a feel for how numbers relate to each other. That feeling helps later with fractions, algebra and science, long after the sums themselves are forgotten.

text: Different scientists invented different temperature scales in the 1700s, and different countries got used to different ones.

The Fahrenheit scale, made in 1724, puts the freezing point of water at 32 degrees and the boiling point at 212. The Celsius scale, made in 1742, puts freezing at 0 and boiling at 100, which is neater. Most of the world, including India, switched to Celsius along with the metric system.

The United States kept Fahrenheit for weather, cooking and [[@body-temperature|fevers]]. A few other places, such as the Bahamas and the Cayman Islands, also use it. Scientists everywhere use Celsius or the Kelvin scale.

st.prompt: A weather report from the US says it will be 86 °F today. What is that in Celsius?

options.t: About 30 °C, a hot day
About 50 °C, dangerously hot
About 10 °C, chilly

st.reveal: To change Fahrenheit to Celsius, subtract 32 and multiply by 5/9. So 86 − 32 = 54, and 54 × 5/9 = 30 °C. A quick rough method is to subtract 30 and halve, which gives 28.

One hand feels warm and the other cool. This is why scientists need thermometers instead of trusting their skin.
myth: Everyone's normal body temperature is exactly 98.6 °F, or 37 °C.

That number comes from a German doctor's measurements in the 1800s. Normal temperature varies from person to person and through the day, and recent studies suggest the average today is a little lower than 37 °C.

sec.t:
Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit was born in 1686 in Danzig, now Gdańsk in Poland, and worked mostly in the Netherlands. He made some of the best [[@thermometer|thermometers]] of his time, and he was among the first to use mercury inside them.

For his zero, he chose the coldest temperature he could reliably make in his workshop: a mixture of ice, water and a salt called ammonium chloride. He then used other fixed points, including the temperature of the human body. After some adjustments, water ended up freezing at 32 degrees and boiling at 212, with 180 degrees in between.

His scale spread through the Netherlands and Britain, and from Britain to its colonies, including America and India.

Cold has a limit. As things cool, their [[atom|atoms]] move more slowly. At about −273.15 °C, atoms would have the least movement possible. This is called absolute zero.

In 1848, the British scientist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed a scale starting there. The Kelvin scale uses the same size of degree as Celsius, but its zero is absolute zero. Water freezes at about 273 kelvin. Scientists use it because it has no [[@negative-numbers|negative numbers]]. Nothing can be colder than zero.

To change Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32. So 30 °C is 86 °F. To go the other way, subtract 32 and multiply by 5/9.

The two scales cross at one point: −40 degrees is the same in both. Very cold places, like parts of Siberia and [[@canada|Canada]], sometimes reach that temperature.

Even in Celsius countries, Fahrenheit hangs around. In India, many people still check a fever in Fahrenheit and know that about 98.6 °F is normal. Doctors and older fever thermometers often use it.

That 98.6 comes from a German doctor, Carl Wunderlich, who published his measurements in 1868. He found an average of 37 °C, which is 98.6 °F. A 2020 study in the United States suggested the average there has slowly fallen since then, to a little below 37 °C. Normal temperature also varies from person to person and through the day, so if you feel unwell, a trusted adult or doctor is the best judge.

Weather can be extreme in either scale. In May 2016, Phalodi in Rajasthan recorded 51 °C, India's highest temperature on record. That's about 124 °F, hot enough to make [[@deserts-sand|desert]] sand painful to touch.

text: A film festival is a gathering where new films are shown, often for the first time anywhere. Directors, actors, critics, film buyers and fans come together for a week or two of screenings, talks and parties. Many festivals have a jury that hands out prizes.

Festivals help small films find an audience. A film made on a tiny budget in a village can win a prize, get bought by a distributor and end up in cinemas or on streaming services worldwide. For many famous directors, a festival screening was the moment their career took off.

st.reveal: Cannes is mainly for people who work in films, such as directors, buyers, critics and journalists, who need a badge. The public can see some free screenings on the beach. Many other festivals, like Toronto, sell tickets to anyone.

sec.t:
Mornings often begin with press screenings for critics, who rush out to write reviews. In the evenings come premieres, where the director and cast walk a red carpet in front of photographers before the film starts.

After a screening, there might be a question-and-answer session with the filmmakers. At Cannes, a much-loved film can get a standing ovation lasting several minutes. Behind the scenes, there is also a film market, where companies buy the rights to show films in different countries. Many films need [[@dubbing-subtitles|subtitles]] to be shown abroad, so festivals help them travel.

In 1956 [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]]'s *Pather Panchali*, about a poor family in a Bengal village, won an award at Cannes. Critics around the world started paying attention to Indian films. Ray went on to win prizes in Berlin and Venice too.

In 2024 Payal Kapadia's *All We Imagine as Light*, about nurses living in Mumbai, won the Grand Prix at Cannes, its second-highest award. It was the first Indian film in the main competition there in 30 years.

India runs festivals of its own. The International Film Festival of India began in 1952 and has been held in [[@goa|Goa]] since 2004. Its top prize is the Golden Peacock. Kerala, Kolkata and Mumbai hold big festivals too.

Many festivals now have sections just for children. Some, like the Giffoni festival in Italy, let children sit on the jury and choose the winners. India has its own children's film festival, whose prize is the Golden Elephant.

Short films, documentaries and [[@animation-how|animation]] get their own festivals as well, such as Annecy in France for animated films. Some school film clubs in India and the US send pupils' short films to youth festivals, and a few have won prizes against adults.

Big studios can fill cinemas with adverts. Small filmmakers can't. A festival gives them a stage, judges who watch closely and journalists who write about what they find. A film in Marathi, Persian or Korean can reach people who would never have heard of it.

Festivals have critics too. Some say they favour a small circle of famous directors, or that tickets and travel cost too much for ordinary film lovers. But for a first-time director, getting a film chosen at all can change everything.

text: Kho-kho is a chasing game from India played by two teams. One team chases and the other defends. Eight chasers sit or squat in a line down the middle of a long court, facing alternate directions. A ninth chaser is the active one, running after the defenders.

The active chaser cannot turn back or cut across the middle line. To change direction, they touch a seated teammate on the back and shout "kho". That teammate leaps up and takes over the chase. Defenders come on three at a time, and each one tagged is out.

options.t: Tap a seated teammate facing the other way and say "kho"
Turn around and run after the defender

st.reveal: A chaser cannot reverse direction once committed. Instead, they give a "kho" to a seated teammate facing the right way, who jumps up and takes over the chase.

d.try: Play a tiny version with six friends in a safe open space. Four sit in a row facing alternate ways, one chases and one runs. The chaser may not turn back but can tap a sitter and shout "kho" to swap. Notice how quickly the chase changes direction.

It is popular in Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, and has federations in many other countries. Teams from about two dozen nations took part in the 2025 World Cup.

sec.t:
The court is a rectangle, about 27 metres long and 16 metres wide for adults, longer than a cricket pitch is from stumps to stumps. A central lane runs down the middle with a wooden pole at each end. The eight seated chasers fill squares along that lane.

The poles are the only places where a chaser can turn around. A clever chaser uses them to swing round the end of the line and surprise a defender from behind.

Kho-kho is much more than running fast. Chasers plan "kho" chains, passing the chase down the line faster than a defender can sprint. A good team corners defenders between two chasers coming from opposite directions.

Defenders practise sudden stops and turns. They watch the seated players closely, because the next chaser could spring up from anywhere. Diving and stretching to tag a defender, called a pole dive or a sky dive, can look like a [[@gymnastics|gymnastics]] move. All this needs powerful leg [[@muscles|muscles]] and quick thinking.

Children across India have played chasing games like kho-kho for generations. The first written rules were drawn up in 1914 by the Deccan Gymkhana, a sports club in [[@pune|Pune]]. In 1936 a group from Amravati demonstrated kho-kho, along with [[@kabaddi|kabaddi]], at the Berlin [[@olympics|Olympics]].

The Kho Kho Federation of India was founded in 1955, and national championships followed. The game is played in schools across Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala and beyond. It is also a medal sport at India's national school games.

In 2022 a professional league, Ultimate Kho Kho, started. It changed the game for television with shorter turns, a smaller squad on court and bonus points for exciting play. Players who had played on mud grounds suddenly appeared on prime-time screens.

In January 2025, New Delhi hosted [[@sport-kho-kho-world|the first Kho Kho World Cup]], with teams from about two dozen countries. India won both the men's and women's titles, beating [[@nepal|Nepal]] in both finals. A game once played in school yards, with nothing but chalk lines and two sticks, now has a world champion.

text: A spinning top stays upright because of its spin. Anything that spins has [[momentum|momentum]] going round in a circle, and it resists being tilted. When [[gravity|gravity]] tries to tip a fast top over, the top doesn't fall. It leans and slowly swings its tilt around in a circle instead.

A yo-yo uses spin as well. As it drops down its string, falling turns into spinning. At the bottom, the spinning yo-yo winds itself back up the string, or "sleeps" there, still whirling. Both toys stop for the same reason: [[@friction|friction]] slowly steals their spin.

options.t: Friction slows its spin until it can't stay upright
The air pushes it over
It runs out of the energy stored in the wood

st.reveal: Friction at the tip and from the air slowly steals the top's spin. As it slows, gravity's pull wins, the wobble grows wider, and the top tips over.

myth: A spinning top stays up because spinning cancels out gravity.
Gravity pulls on a spinning top just as hard as on a still one. The spin turns that pull into a slow sideways wobble, called precession, instead of a fall. Once the spin fades, the top tips over.

sec.t:
In India, a classic lattu is a pear-shaped wooden top with an iron nail for a tip. You wind a string tightly around it, then fling it down and pull. The string unwinds and sets the top spinning on the ground. Expert players can scoop a spinning lattu onto a palm, still turning.

In Tamil Nadu the top is called a bambaram, and every region has its own name and games. One common game has players try to hit an opponent's top out of a chalk circle. Craftspeople in Channapatna, Karnataka, make brightly lacquered [[@channapatna-toys|wooden tops]] as well.

A yo-yo is two discs joined by a short axle, with a string looped around it. When you let go, it falls and spins faster and faster. At the bottom, all the energy of falling has turned into spin.

On a simple yo-yo, the string is tied tight to the axle. The spinning yo-yo winds itself back up, almost to your hand. Each trip loses a little energy to [[friction|friction]], so you give a small tug to help.

Modern yo-yos have a loose loop around a smooth ball bearing. At the bottom they "sleep", spinning in place. A sharp tug makes the string grip again, and up it comes.

Hold a yo-yo at your hand and it has stored energy, because gravity can pull it down. As it falls, that stored energy turns into two kinds of motion: dropping and spinning. A heavy rim helps, which is why many yo-yos put most of their weight near the edge.

A top gets its energy from your throw and the pull of the string. From then on it only loses energy. Some escapes as a faint scratch of sound, some as warmth at the tip, and some pushing through the air. A top with a smooth, hard point on a polished floor can spin for minutes. On rough cement it gives up far sooner.

sec.h: An old toy that keeps coming back
sec.t:
A painted Greek cup from about 440 BCE shows a boy with a disc on a string. In the 1920s, Pedro Flores, a Filipino immigrant in California, started a company making yo-yos. A businessman named Donald Duncan bought it, and yo-yo contests spread across the USA.

Tops are probably even older, and children on every continent have spun them. Spin a ball, a coin, or a plate on a stick, and you meet the same idea that kept the first lattu steady.

text: Sleepwalking happens when part of the brain wakes up while the rest stays deeply asleep. The parts that control walking and simple actions switch on. The parts that handle thinking, judgement and memory stay switched off.

So a sleepwalker can sit up, walk around, open doors and even talk, often with their eyes wide open. But they are not really aware of what they are doing, and they usually remember nothing the next morning.
It is much more common in children than adults. Most children who sleepwalk grow out of it by their teenage years.

sec.t:
Sleep comes in cycles, each about 90 minutes long. In each cycle, you drift from light sleep into deep sleep, then into dreaming sleep, called REM sleep, when your eyes flick around under your lids.

Sleepwalking almost always happens in deep sleep, usually in the first few hours of the night. Something partly wakes the brain, perhaps a noise or a full bladder, but it fails to wake up fully. The brain gets stuck in between, one foot in sleep and one in waking.

During REM sleep, your body is mostly paralysed, so you cannot act out [[@dreams|dreams]]. That's why sleepwalkers are usually not acting out a dream. They are doing simple, automatic things.

Most sleepwalking is calm. Children might sit up, look around and lie down again. Some walk to another room, or to the kitchen, or try to get dressed. Many mumble or talk, though what they say often makes little sense.

Their eyes are usually open but glassy, and they may look straight through you. They move more clumsily than when awake. An episode can last from a few seconds to half an hour, then the person goes back to bed, often on their own.

Because they are not fully aware, sleepwalkers can hurt themselves on stairs, doors or windows. Families of regular sleepwalkers often lock outside doors, put gates on stairs and clear toys from the floor at night.

sec.h: Why some people and not others
sec.t:
Sleepwalking runs in families. If a parent sleepwalked as a child, their children are much more likely to as well. Scientists think [[gene|genes]] affect how easily the brain gets stuck in between sleep and waking.

Children sleepwalk more partly because they spend more time in deep sleep than adults. Their brains are still developing the switches that move smoothly from one sleep stage to another.

Several things make episodes more likely. The biggest is not getting enough [[@sleep-why|sleep]], followed by going to bed at irregular times. Fever, stress, noisy bedrooms and a full bladder at night can trigger it too.

Writers have used sleepwalking in stories for centuries. In William Shakespeare's play Macbeth, written around 1606, Lady Macbeth walks in her sleep, rubbing her hands as if trying to wash off a stain only she can see. A doctor and a servant watch her in secret. It is one of the most famous sleepwalking scenes ever written.

Real sleepwalking is usually far less dramatic. Still, doctors have recorded rare cases of sleepwalkers who cooked whole meals or even drove a car.

For most children, sleepwalking is harmless and fades with age. Simple things often help: a regular bedtime, enough sleep, a calm routine before bed and going to the toilet before lights out.

It is worth talking to a parent and a doctor if sleepwalking happens very often, if the person gets hurt or leaves the house, or if it starts in adulthood. A doctor might check for problems like snoring or breathing pauses that disturb sleep. Humans are built to be still and safe in the dark, unlike the [[@nocturnal-animals|nocturnal animals]] that do their busiest living at night.

text: Fear is your body's alarm system. When you sense danger, such as a loud bang, a growling dog or a sudden drop, a part of your brain called the [[amygdala|amygdala]] sounds the alarm. Within moments, your body gets ready to act. Your heart pounds, you breathe faster, your muscles tense and your senses sharpen.

This response helped our ancestors survive. Someone who froze or ran at the first sign of a lion was more likely to live long enough to have children. Today, the same system kicks in before an exam or a scary film. It isn't always helpful, but it is completely normal, and there are good ways to calm it down.

st.reveal: In a fright, your body puts digestion on hold and sends more blood to your muscles, heart and lungs, ready to act. The sudden change in your gut can feel like butterflies or a knot.

myth: Brave people don't feel fear.

sec.h: The fast road and the slow road
sec.t:
Your eyes and ears send signals to a relay station deep in the brain. From there, the signals take two paths. One goes straight to the amygdala, quickly and roughly. The other goes up to the outer layer of the brain, where you think things through, which is slower but more accurate.

The scientist Joseph LeDoux called these the "low road" and the "high road". The low road lets you jump back from a curved stick before you even know whether it's a snake. A split second later, the high road catches up and tells you it's just a stick, and you feel a little silly. It's better to be silly than bitten.

Babies seem to come ready to fear a few things, such as loud noises and falling. In a famous 1960 experiment called the visual cliff, crawling babies were placed on a glass table with what looked like a sudden drop underneath. Most would not crawl over the "edge", even when their mothers called them.

Many other fears are learned. In experiments, young monkeys raised in a lab weren't afraid of [[@snakes-venom|snakes]] at first. After watching a video of another monkey reacting with terror to a snake, they quickly became afraid too. Interestingly, they did not learn to fear flowers the same way, which suggests our brains are primed to learn some fears faster than others.

Scientists learned a lot from a woman known as S.M. A rare disease damaged both sides of her amygdala. Researchers took her to a pet shop with snakes and spiders, to a "haunted house" and showed her scary films. She stayed calm and curious, and even tried to touch a snake.

It sounds like a superpower, but it isn't. S.M. has walked into dangerous situations that most people would avoid. Fear, uncomfortable as it is, keeps us safe.

Sometimes fear rings too loudly, or at things that aren't really dangerous. A fear that's very strong and hard to control, like a terror of lifts or dogs, is called a phobia. Psychologists often help people face such fears in small, safe steps until the alarm quietens down.

For everyday fears, slow breathing helps, especially breathing out for longer than you breathe in. Naming the feeling ("I'm nervous") can calm the amygdala a little. Talking to a trusted adult helps too. And some people enjoy a safe scare, on a [[@theme-parks|roller coaster]] or with a ghost story, because the rush is followed by relief.

text: Around one person in ten prefers to use their left hand for writing, throwing and eating. It's been about the same through history and across the world. Nobody fully knows why.

[[gene|Genes]] play a part. Left-handed parents are a little more likely to have left-handed children. But scientists haven't found a single left-handed gene. Instead, many genes each seem to nudge the odds a tiny bit. Things that happen as a baby grows in the womb matter too. Even identical twins, who share the same genes, are sometimes one left-handed and one right-handed. So handedness seems to be part inheritance and part chance.

sec.t:
Hand preference starts early. In the early 1990s, a team in Northern Ireland led by Peter Hepper watched babies in the womb using [[ultrasound|ultrasound]] scans. Most of them sucked their right thumb. Years later, the team checked on some of those children. Those who had sucked their right thumb had grown up right-handed. Those who had sucked their left were much more likely to be left-handed.

Most toddlers try both hands for a while. A clear preference usually shows by about age 2 to 4. Your [[@brain-works|brain]] is wired so that its left half controls the right side of the body, and the right half controls the left. How that links to [[@handedness-brain|handedness]] is still being worked out.

For centuries, many people saw left-handedness as something to fix. The Latin word for left, sinister, came to mean evil in English. In many schools in Britain, the USA and India, left-handed children were made to write with their right hand, sometimes with their left hand tied behind them. In parts of India and many other places, eating with the left hand is still seen as impolite, because it is traditionally kept for washing.

Today, most schools let children use whichever hand comes naturally. Still, much of the world is built for right-handers: scissors, can openers, school desks with the writing arm on the right. Left-handers writing in English or Hindi move their hand across fresh ink, which is why many hook their wrist. With some [[@writing-tools|writing tools]], like fountain pens, smudges are a real problem.

In one-on-one sports, left-handers turn up much more than one in ten. Many great [[@tennis|tennis]] players, boxers and fencers have been left-handed. In cricket, left-handed batters such as Brian Lara and Sourav Ganguly gave bowlers headaches, because the ball's angle and the fielding positions are reversed.

The reason is surprise. Most players spend their lives facing right-handers. A left-hander's shots come from unexpected angles. Some scientists think this advantage in fights and games may be one reason left-handedness has never died out. International Left-Handers Day, on 13 August, has been marked since 1976.

text: Skin gets its colour mainly from [[melanin|melanin]], a [[pigment|pigment]] made by special cells called melanocytes. More melanin, and especially more of the dark brown kind, makes skin darker. Less makes it lighter.

The amount your body makes depends on your [[gene|genes]]. Those genes, in turn, were shaped by sunlight. Over tens of thousands of years, people whose ancestors lived where the sun is fierce, near the [[equator|equator]], kept dark skin. People whose ancestors moved to cloudier, cooler places far from the equator often became lighter. Skin colour is mainly a record of how much sunshine your great-great-great-grandparents lived under.

options.t: About the same number
About twice as many
About ten times as many

st.reveal: People of all skin colours have roughly the same number of melanocytes. In darker skin, they make more melanin, more of the dark kind, and pack it into bigger bundles.

src: Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History, Human Origins Program, Human skin colour variation.

d.try: Put two identical sheets of coloured paper in a sunny window, and cover half of one with a book. After a week, compare the covered and uncovered parts. Sunlight fades dyes in paper by breaking them down, and in skin it can break down useful chemicals too, which melanin helps to block.
myth: People with dark skin can't get sunburnt, so they never need sun protection.
Dark skin has more natural protection, but it can still burn in strong sun, especially at high altitude or near water. Everyone's skin can be damaged by too much ultraviolet light.

sec.t:
At the bottom of the outer layer of your [[@skin|skin]] sit the melanocytes. They have long arms, like tiny octopuses, that hand packets of melanin to the skin cells around them. Those packets settle over each cell's centre like a sunshade, guarding its DNA from damage.

There are two main kinds of melanin. Eumelanin is brown to black. Pheomelanin is a lighter red to yellow, and people with red hair and freckles have a lot of it. Everyone's skin colour comes from a mix of the two, plus a little help from blood near the surface, which adds pink.

When strong sun hits your skin, melanocytes speed up and make more melanin. That's a tan. It takes a few days to appear, and it fades once you stay indoors. A tan gives only a little extra protection, roughly like a very weak sunscreen, so it is no excuse to bake in the sun.

Sunlight brings both harm and help. Its [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] rays can burn skin and break down folate, a B [[vitamin|vitamin]] the body needs for growing babies and healthy cells. But the same rays let skin make vitamin D, which keeps bones strong.

Scientists such as the American anthropologist Nina Jablonski think skin colour [[evolve|evolved]] as a balance between the two. Our early ancestors in Africa lost most of their body hair and developed dark skin to protect their folate under a strong sun. As some groups spread into Europe and northern Asia, where the sun is weaker, lighter skin helped them make enough vitamin D.

There are interesting exceptions. The Inuit of the Arctic have fairly dark skin for such a sunless place, possibly because their traditional diet of fish and seal is rich in vitamin D.

{{story:human-evolution}}

Skin colour isn't controlled by one switch. Dozens of [[@genes-family|genes]] each nudge it a little lighter or darker, which is why children can have a different shade from either parent, and why brothers and sisters can look quite different.

Skin tone is also a poor guide to ancestry. Scientists have found more genetic variety among people in Africa than among people on all other continents put together. Two people with similar skin may share less DNA than two people whose skin looks completely different.

India has an enormous range of skin tones, from very light to very dark. You can see that range within a single city, a single school or even a single family. Like many countries, it also has a long history of treating lighter skin as more beautiful. In 2020, after criticism, one of the country's best-known fairness creams changed its name to drop the word "fair".

Scientists see no shade as better or worse than any other. Each is a smart answer to a different amount of sunshine. Whatever your colour, sunlight still matters, so shade and [[@sunburn-sunscreen|sunscreen]] on very sunny days make sense for everyone.

text: Most of your body is water. It's in your blood, inside every cell and in the spaces between them. Water carries food and oxygen around your body, and carries waste away. It cushions your brain and joints, keeps your eyes moist and lets you [[@sweat|sweat]] to cool down. Almost every chemical reaction that keeps you alive happens in water.

And you lose water all day: in urine, in sweat, even in every breath you breathe out. If you don't replace it, your blood gets thicker, your heart works harder and your brain gets less efficient. So you need to keep topping up, from drinks and from food.
