st.reveal: All drinks count, and so does food. Fruit like watermelon is more than 90% water, and dal, rice, curd and vegetables all carry water too. About a fifth of the water you take in comes from what you eat.

myth: Everyone must drink exactly eight glasses of water a day.
There's no single magic number. How much you need depends on your size, how active you are and the weather, and food provides part of it. Thirst and pale-yellow urine are good everyday guides.

sec.h: How your body keeps the level right
sec.t:
Your body is very good at balancing its water. When you've lost even a little, your blood becomes slightly saltier. A part of [[@brain-works|the brain]] called the hypothalamus notices this and does two things. It makes you feel thirsty. And it sends a [[hormone|hormone]] to your [[@kidneys|kidneys]] telling them to save water, so your urine gets darker and smaller in amount.

When you drink more than you need, the kidneys let more go, and your urine turns pale. That's why the colour of your wee is a handy guide. Pale straw is good. Dark yellow usually means drink more.

You may have heard that everyone must drink eight glasses of water a day. Nobody is quite sure where this began, but a 1945 report in the USA suggested about 2.5 litres a day for adults. The next sentence said that most of this comes from food, and people seem to have forgotten it.

Children of around ten need roughly 1.5 litres of drinks a day, more in hot weather or after sport. Water and milk are the best choices. Sugary drinks give water too, but also a lot of sugar. Drinking far too much water very quickly can be dangerous, though this is rare and mostly happens to adults in long [[endurance|endurance]] races.

For your body, the water has to be clean. Germs in dirty water cause illnesses like cholera and typhoid. Around the world, about 2 billion people still don't have safe drinking water at home. India's Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019, aims to bring a tap connection to every rural home.

Cities clean water by filtering it and adding small amounts of chlorine. At home, many families in India [[@water-purify|boil or filter]] water before drinking. In much of the USA, tap water is treated so it's safe to drink straight away. The water in your glass has travelled through clouds, rivers and underground rock, round and round the [[@water-cycle|water cycle]], for billions of years.

text: Great Zimbabwe was a stone city in southern Africa, built between about 1100 and 1450. It was the capital of a powerful kingdom whose rulers grew rich from cattle and from trading gold and ivory. At its height, perhaps more than 10,000 people lived there, though estimates vary a lot.

Its builders were ancestors of the Shona people, who still live in the region. They raised huge walls of [[granite|granite]] blocks without any mortar, and many still stand today. The country of Zimbabwe, which became independent in 1980, took its name from these ruins. In the Shona language, "dzimba dza mabwe" means "houses of stone".

st.prompt: How did the builders of Great Zimbabwe hold their stone walls together?

options.t: They shaped the stones to fit tightly, with no mortar at all
They used a kind of early cement
They drilled holes and joined the stones with iron pins

st.reveal: The builders split granite into neat blocks and stacked them carefully, each layer slightly set back from the one below. The weight and fit hold the walls together, and many have stood for over 600 years.

n.certNote: Archaeologists agree that Great Zimbabwe was built by ancestors of the Shona people between about 1100 and 1450. How many people lived there, and exactly why it declined, are still debated.

d.try: Build two small walls from sugar cubes, wooden blocks or Lego bricks. In one, stack the blocks straight up in columns. In the other, stagger them like real bricks, so each block sits over a joint below. Push both gently from the side and see which holds.
myth: Great Zimbabwe was built by foreigners, such as the Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba, not by Africans.

These claims were made by European colonists in the 1800s and 1900s and have been disproved. Archaeology, dating and local history all show that the city was built by the ancestors of the Shona people.

sec.t:
The most famous part of the site is the Great Enclosure, a huge oval wall up to about 11 m high and roughly 250 m around. It's the largest ancient stone structure in Africa south of the Sahara.

The builders split granite from nearby hills into flat blocks, then stacked them in neat rows without any mortar. Each layer sits slightly back from the one below, so the wall leans gently inwards and stays stable. The top is decorated in places with a zigzag pattern.

Inside stands a solid stone tower shaped like a cone, about 10 m tall. Nobody knows exactly what it was for. It may have been a symbol of the king's power, or a sign of plenty, like a giant grain store.

sec.h: Gold, beads and the Indian Ocean
sec.t:
Great Zimbabwe's kings controlled the trade in gold mined on the plateau around them. Traders carried gold and ivory east to ports on the Indian Ocean coast, such as Sofala and Kilwa. Merchants from the Swahili coast sailed these goods north and east across the ocean, using the [[monsoon|monsoon]] winds.

In return, [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] have found glass beads from India, pottery from China and Persia, and a coin from Kilwa at the site. Great Zimbabwe was part of a [[@trade-routes|trade network]] that linked the African interior with India, Arabia and China.

Eight carved birds made of soapstone, each on top of a tall pillar, were found at the site. They don't look like any one real bird, though some people see an eagle in them. They may have stood for the spirits of royal ancestors.

Several were taken to South Africa and elsewhere in [[colonial|colonial]] times. Most have now been returned. The Zimbabwe bird appears on the country's [[@flags|flag]] and coat of arms.

When European visitors reached Great Zimbabwe in the late 1800s, many refused to believe Africans had built it. Some claimed it was the work of the [[@phoenicians|Phoenicians]], or the palace of the Queen of Sheba. These ideas helped colonists argue that Africans had no history of their own.

In 1905 the [[archaeologist|archaeologist]] David Randall-MacIver, and in 1929 Gertrude Caton-Thompson, studied the site carefully. Both concluded it was African. The white-minority government of Rhodesia still pressured guides and museums to stay vague about this until 1980.

By about 1450, Great Zimbabwe was being abandoned. Possible reasons include too many people and cattle for the land, [[drought|droughts]] and shifting trade routes. Power moved to other kingdoms nearby, such as Mutapa and Khami. Like [[@mali-empire|Mali]] in West Africa, it was a rich trading state that the outside world long ignored. Its walls are still there to prove it was real.

text: In the 1630s, tulips became a status symbol in the Dutch Republic, now the Netherlands. The country was rich from trade, and owning rare, beautiful flowers showed off taste and wealth. The most prized tulips had striking flame-like stripes, and nobody could grow them on demand.

Prices climbed and climbed. By the winter of 1636–37, people were trading contracts for bulbs still buried in the ground, sometimes reselling them several times in a day. In February 1637 buyers suddenly stopped turning up, and prices collapsed. The episode became famous as "tulip mania", often called the first big price bubble in history.

st.prompt: In the 1630s, most tulip deals in the Netherlands were made in winter. What were people actually buying?

options.t: Fresh cut flowers in vases
Promises to receive bulbs that were still buried in the ground
Paintings of tulips

st.reveal: Tulips bloom in spring and bulbs can only be dug up in summer. So in winter people signed contracts for bulbs still underground. Some contracts were bought and sold again and again without anyone seeing a flower.

src.Anne Goldgar, Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age (University of Chicago Press, 2007).

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, tulip mania.
n.certNote: Prices really did soar and then crash in early 1637. But many famous stories about ruined families come from pamphlets written to scold people, and historians now think the damage was much smaller than legend says.

myth: Tulip mania ruined the Dutch economy and drove many people to despair.

Historians who studied records from the time found little sign of widespread ruin. Most buyers were fairly well-off merchants and craftspeople, and many contracts were simply cancelled. The Dutch economy kept growing through the 1600s.

sec.t:
Tulips are not originally Dutch. They grew wild in the mountains of Central Asia and were grown in gardens across the [[@ottomans|Ottoman Empire]]. In Turkish, the tulip is lale, and it decorated tiles, clothes and palaces in Istanbul.

In the 1590s, a [[botanist|botanist]] named Carolus Clusius planted tulips in the university garden at Leiden. They were new and dazzling in northern Europe, with colours stronger than any local flower. Wealthy collectors wanted them, and some bulbs were stolen from Clusius's garden.

The most valuable tulips were called "broken". Their petals had feathery stripes of red or purple on white or yellow, like flames. The most famous was Semper Augustus, red and white. Only a handful were known.

Nobody could predict which bulbs would break. A plain tulip might grow striped the next year, or never. Then the striped ones tended to grow weaker. In the 1920s scientists discovered why: the stripes were caused by a virus, spread from plant to plant by aphids. The disease made them beautiful and fragile at the same time.

In early February 1637, at a bulb auction in Haarlem, buyers simply didn't bid. Word spread fast. Within days, nobody wanted to pay the old prices. People who had promised to buy bulbs at high prices refused to pay. Courts were unwilling to enforce the contracts, and many deals were settled for a small fraction or cancelled.

This is how many bubbles end, with prices driven by [[@supply-demand|supply and demand]] and by people expecting someone else to pay more later. When that belief vanishes, prices fall fast.

For centuries, tulip mania was told as a warning tale. A popular 1841 book by Charles Mackay described people selling homes and farms, and a sailor who ate a priceless bulb thinking it was an onion. Much of this came from moralising songs and pamphlets of the 1630s.

The historian Anne Goldgar searched Dutch records and found few signs of mass ruin. Buyers were mostly fairly well-off, and the Dutch [[economy|economy]] carried on growing.

The Netherlands is still famous for tulips, grown in huge colourful fields. Keukenhof gardens near Leiden plant around 7 million bulbs each year. India has its own tulip spectacle. In [[@kashmir|Kashmir]], the Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden in Srinagar, Asia's largest, displayed about 1.7 million tulips in 2025. And the country that grows the most is the same one that has pushed back the sea, as the story of how the [[@world-netherlands-water|Dutch live below sea level]] explains.

text: Scotland is one of the four countries that make up the United Kingdom, along with England, Wales and Northern Ireland. It covers the northern third of the island of Great Britain, plus nearly 800 islands. Its capital is Edinburgh and its largest city is Glasgow.

Scotland is known for wild mountains and deep lakes, called lochs, castles, bagpipes, kilts and tartan. It is also known for inventors, writers and scientists far out of proportion to its size of about 55 lakh people, fewer than live in Bengaluru. Many Scots speak with a strong accent, and some still speak Scottish Gaelic or Scots.

sec.t:
The north and west of Scotland are the Highlands, a land of bare mountains, moors and long, narrow lochs. Ben Nevis, at 1,345 metres, is the highest mountain in the UK. These mountains are very old. Hundreds of millions of years ago they were part of the same range as the [[@appalachians|Appalachians]] in North America, before the Atlantic Ocean opened and split them apart.

Loch Ness is about 37 kilometres long and over 200 metres deep. It holds more fresh water than all the lakes of England and Wales combined. It is most famous, of course, for Nessie, the monster many visitors hope to glimpse. The best-known "photo" of her, taken in 1934, turned out decades later to be a toy submarine with a model head stuck on top. Searches with sonar and even DNA sampling of the water have found plenty of eels, but no monster.

For a small country, Scotland has produced a surprising number of world-changing ideas. Alexander Graham Bell, born in Edinburgh in 1847, was one of the inventors of the [[@telephone-history|telephone]], which he patented in the USA in 1876. John Logie Baird, from near Glasgow, showed the first working television pictures in London in 1926, part of the story of [[@television-invented|television]].

In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming noticed that mould growing on a dish in his London lab had killed the [[bacteria|bacteria]] around it. That mould gave penicillin, the first widely used [[@antibiotics|antibiotic]]. In 1996, scientists at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh created Dolly the sheep, the first [[mammal|mammal]] cloned from an adult cell.

Highland clans wove woollen cloth in checked patterns called tartans, and many families today have their own tartan. Bagpipes, with a bag of air squeezed under the arm, make a sound loud enough to carry across a glen. Golf grew up on the windy links of the east coast, and St Andrews is called the home of golf.

Scotland's national animal is the [[@myths-unicorns|unicorn]], a legend chosen for its strength and pride. In 2014, Scots voted in a [[referendum|referendum]] on whether to become independent from the UK. About 55 percent voted to stay, and the question is still debated today.

text: Nobody invented punctuation all at once. It was built up over about 2,000 years by many people: librarians in Alexandria, monks in Ireland, scholars at the court of Charlemagne and printers in Venice. Each added marks to solve a problem, and the useful ones stuck.

The earliest Greek and Roman texts were written with no spaces and no punctuation at all, a style called *scriptio continua*. Reading was mostly done aloud, so readers worked out pauses themselves. As more people started reading silently, and in languages that were not their own, they needed help, and dots, spaces and squiggles crept onto the page.

st.reveal: Most reading was done aloud, and readers prepared a text beforehand, working out where sentences began and ended. A few scholars added dots to help, but they were not used by everyone for centuries.

sec.t:
For a long time, Romans thought dots were for beginners. Then, from about the 7th century, monks in Ireland and Britain began copying Latin religious books. Latin was a foreign language to them, so run-together words were a real puzzle. They started leaving spaces between words.

The idea was so useful that it spread across Europe. Scribes at the court of Charlemagne, around 800 CE, also developed a clear new handwriting with small letters, which became the ancestor of the lowercase alphabet you are reading now.

[[medieval|Medieval]] monks sang and chanted their prayers, so many marks were about the voice. A mark called the punctus interrogativus, a dot with a wavy line above, showed that the voice should rise at a question. Over centuries it became the question mark.

The exclamation mark has a similar story. It began as a mark of admiration or wonder, sometimes called the "note of admiration". The popular story that it came from the Latin "io", meaning joy, is probably a legend.

When the [[@printing-press|printing press]] arrived in the 1450s, punctuation began to settle down. In Venice in the 1490s, the printer Aldus Manutius published books using a semicolon, among the first in print. His family also helped make the comma look the way it does today.

Printers wanted every copy to look the same, so they made rules, and schools followed them. Spanish, in 1754, made a different choice: upside-down question marks and exclamation marks at the start of sentences, so readers know early which tone to use. ¿Qué tal?

Indian scripts have their own marks. In Devanagari, used for [[@hindi-language|Hindi]], Marathi and Sanskrit, the full stop is a straight vertical line, the purna viram or danda. Ancient Sanskrit verses used a single line to end half a verse and a double line to end a full one.

Urdu, written right to left, uses a question mark facing the other way. Tamil and Bengali texts have adopted many European marks, such as commas and question marks, since the 1800s.

In 1962, an American advertising man, Martin Speckter, invented the interrobang, a question mark and exclamation mark merged into one, for sentences like "You did what?!". It never caught on, though some typewriters included it.

Today, people punctuate messages with smileys and hearts. Some linguists think [[@emojis|emojis]] work a bit like the old voice marks of medieval monks, telling the reader how a sentence should sound.

text: Many people say food tastes better eaten with their hands, and science suggests there may be something in it. Flavour isn't made only by your tongue. Your brain builds it from taste, smell, sight, sound and touch all at once. When your fingers feel the warmth, softness and texture of food before it reaches your mouth, your brain gets extra information and gets ready to enjoy it.

Eating with hands also changes how you eat. You can mix rice and dal just the way you like, pick out bones and feel when food is too hot. Many people find it slower, more careful and more satisfying. For billions of people, it is simply the normal, best way to eat.

sec.h: Eating with hands around the world
sec.t:
In India, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Pakistan, many people eat most meals by hand. In north India, people often eat rotis with just their fingertips, tearing a piece to scoop up dal or sabzi. In south India, rice is mixed with sambar or rasam using the whole hand and pushed into the mouth with the thumb.

In Ethiopia and Eritrea, meals are served on injera, a large spongy flatbread. Everyone tears off pieces and uses them to pick up stews from a shared plate. In West Africa, balls of fufu are dipped in soup, and in the Middle East, Malaysia and Indonesia, hand-eating is common too.

In many hand-eating cultures, only the right hand touches food. The left hand is kept for washing and other jobs. Even left-handed children are often taught to eat with their right hand, though some families are more relaxed about it today.

Washing is central. Many homes and restaurants in India have a basin near the dining area, and people wash before and after every meal. Soap breaks up the oily layer that holds germs on skin, which is how [[@soap-germs|soap fights germs]].

In south India, festive meals are often served on a banana leaf. Rice, dal, sambar, vegetables, pickles and payasam are placed in a particular order. After eating, many people fold the leaf towards themselves to show they enjoyed the meal, a custom that varies by region and community.

It is a whole way of eating, explored in [[@south-indian-meals|South Indian meals]]. Eating from a leaf with your hands means no plates or cutlery to wash, and the leaf can be composted.

Americans might think hand-eating is unusual, until they think about their favourite foods. Burgers, hot dogs, pizza, fried chicken, corn on the cob and [[@tacos|tacos]] are all usually eaten by hand. Barbecue ribs are almost impossible to eat any other way.

Etiquette guides say hand food should be eaten by hand, because forcing a knife and fork onto a burger is awkward and messy.

Hand-eating isn't the old way waiting to be replaced by cutlery. It is a different tradition with its own rules and skills. Many families mix both, eating rice by hand and using a spoon for curd or ice cream.

Knives, forks and spoons have their own long and surprising history. The fork, in particular, was once seen in Europe as a ridiculous luxury, a story told in [[@food-cutlery-history|when people started using forks]].

text: Each popcorn kernel holds a tiny drop of water inside a hard, waterproof shell called the hull. When you heat the kernel, that water turns into steam. The steam can't escape, so the pressure inside keeps rising.

At about 180°C, the hull can't take it any more and bursts open. In a fraction of a second, the soft [[starch|starch]] inside, heated and squeezed by the steam, puffs out into a white foam. It cools and sets almost instantly into the fluffy shape you eat. The kernel turns inside out and grows many times bigger.

sec.h: A pressure cooker in a seed
sec.t:
A popcorn kernel works much like a [[@pressure-cooker|pressure cooker]]. The water inside it gets hotter than the usual boiling point of 100°C, because the hull keeps it under pressure. Just before it bursts, the pressure inside is roughly nine times that of the air around you.

When the hull breaks, the pressure drops suddenly. The super-hot water flashes into steam all at once, blowing up the starch like a balloon. That's why the kernel pops instead of slowly cooking.

Every bowl has a few hard kernels left at the bottom. Some didn't have enough water inside them, perhaps because they dried out in storage. Others had a tiny crack in their hull, so steam leaked out slowly and pressure never built up.

Popcorn makers store kernels carefully so they keep just the right amount of moisture, about 14%. Too dry, and they won't pop. Too wet, and they pop into chewy, small pieces. Popped kernels come in two main shapes. "Butterfly" popcorn has wings that catch salt and butter, while round "mushroom" popcorn is tougher, so it is used for caramel coatings.

In 2015, two French scientists filmed popcorn at thousands of frames a second. They saw that the starch bursting out pushes against the pan like a little leg, making the kernel jump into the air.

They also found that the pop doesn't come from the hull breaking. It happens when steam suddenly rushes out of the kernel, a bit like the pop of a cork. Each kernel pops at a slightly different moment, which is why you hear a crackle.

[[@corn-maize|Maize]] was first farmed in [[@mexico|Mexico]] about 9,000 years ago. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] found corn cobs in [[@peru|Peru]], about 6,700 years old, that show signs of being popped. People of the Americas have eaten popcorn for thousands of years.

India has popping foods too. Jowar can be popped, and puffed rice, called murmura, is made by heating rice grains until their moisture puffs them up. Phool makhana, the seeds of a water lily grown in Bihar, are roasted until they pop.

text: Sushi is a Japanese dish made with short-grain [[@rice|rice]] seasoned with vinegar, a little sugar and salt. That rice is the heart of it. It is then pressed into small bite-sized blocks with a slice of fish on top, rolled up in [[@seaweed-food|sheets of seaweed]], or packed into little cones.

Many people think sushi means raw fish, but it does not. Raw fish without rice is called sashimi. Sushi can be made with cooked prawns, grilled eel, sweet omelette, cucumber or pickled radish. In Japan, it is often a special-occasion meal, eaten with soy sauce, a dab of wasabi and slices of pink pickled ginger. Real wasabi is a rare, costly root, so the green paste served outside Japan is usually horseradish and mustard, dyed green.

sec.t:
Sushi began as a way to [[@food-preserve|preserve food]]. More than a thousand years ago, in parts of South-East Asia, China and then Japan, people packed cleaned fish in cooked rice and left it for months. The rice fermented and turned sour, and the [[acid|acid]] stopped the fish from spoiling. When it was time to eat, they threw the rice away and ate the fish.

In Japan, one ancient form, called narezushi, is still made today near Lake Biwa. Over the centuries, people began eating the rice too, and fermenting it for shorter times.

Rolled sushi, called maki, is wrapped in nori. Nori is made from a red seaweed that grows on nets in shallow coastal water. It is chopped, spread thin on frames like paper, and dried into dark green sheets.

A sushi chef lays nori on a bamboo mat, spreads rice over it, adds a line of filling and rolls it into a tight log before slicing. Inside-out rolls, with rice on the outside, became popular in the United States. The California roll, with crab and avocado, was made for American diners who were nervous about seaweed and raw fish. Several chefs in Los Angeles and Vancouver claim to have invented it.

Fish meant to be eaten raw has to be very fresh and handled with great care. Many countries require or advise that it be frozen solid for a set time first, which kills tiny [[parasite|parasites]]. Good sushi restaurants buy fish from trusted suppliers and keep it cold all the way.

Young children, pregnant women and people who are unwell are often told to stick to cooked or vegetarian sushi. It is a sensible question to ask an adult before trying it.

Sushi has become popular in Indian cities over the past twenty years or so, first in big hotels and then in malls and delivery apps. Indian chefs quickly made it their own, with rolls of paneer, mango, avocado or spicy tempura vegetables for vegetarian diners. Some even add a hint of chilli to the mayonnaise, which a sushi chef in Tokyo might find very surprising.
